facts.claim: Acute mountain sickness is a headache with one or more of: loss of appetite, nausea or vomiting, fatigue or weakness, dizziness or lightheadedness.

source.title: WMS: Acute Altitude Illness Clinical Practice Guideline, 2024 Update, summary → AMS/HACE Diagnosis
CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → Acute mountain sickness

facts.claim: Altitude illness is a risk from about this altitude upwards, and sometimes lower.

source.title: WMS: Acute Altitude Illness Clinical Practice Guideline, 2024 Update, summary → Introduction
CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → Risk to travelers

facts.claim: The symptoms of acute mountain sickness begin this many hours after arriving at a new altitude, often during or after the first night.

source.title: CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → Acute mountain sickness → Diagnosis

versions.note: Within several hours to 3 days of the ascent.

source.title: WMS: Acute Altitude Illness Clinical Practice Guideline, 2024 Update, summary → AMS/HACE Diagnosis

facts.claim: With acute mountain sickness of any severity, a climber stops going up and rests at the same altitude, and goes on only once the symptoms have gone; if they get worse in spite of treatment, the climber descends.

source.title: WMS: Acute Altitude Illness Clinical Practice Guideline, 2024 Update, summary → AMS/HACE Treatment
CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → Acute mountain sickness → Treatment

facts.claim: A climber with symptoms of altitude illness never goes higher, nor back up to an altitude reached before.

source.title: WMS: Acute Altitude Illness Clinical Practice Guideline, 2024 Update, summary → AMS/HACE Treatment

versions.note: Never up to sleep at a higher altitude.

source.title: CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → Preventing severe altitude illness or death

facts.claim: Descending at least this far relieves acute mountain sickness quickly, the more so with little exertion.

source.title: CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → Acute mountain sickness → Treatment

facts.claim: High-altitude cerebral edema is the severe end of acute mountain sickness: ataxia (lost coordination, an unsteady walk), often the first sign, and an altered mind (confusion, drowsiness), going on to coma.

source.title: WMS: Acute Altitude Illness Clinical Practice Guideline, 2024 Update, summary → AMS/HACE Diagnosis
CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → High-altitude cerebral edema

facts.claim: Ataxia is gauged by having the climber walk heel to toe.

source.title: WMS: Acute Altitude Illness Clinical Practice Guideline, 2024 Update, summary → AMS/HACE Diagnosis

facts.claim: High-altitude cerebral edema requires immediate descent: without treatment or descent, coma is likely within 12–24 hours of the onset of ataxia.

source.title: CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → High-altitude cerebral edema → Treatment

versions.note: Descent at any suspicion of cerebral edema; no time to coma given.

source.title: WMS: Acute Altitude Illness Clinical Practice Guideline, 2024 Update, summary → AMS/HACE Treatment

facts.claim: High-altitude pulmonary edema begins as breathlessness on exertion beyond what the climber has known at altitude, with a dry cough, weakness and a gurgling in the chest; as it goes on, the climber is breathless at rest, may turn blue and may cough up pink, frothy sputum.

source.title: WMS: Acute Altitude Illness Clinical Practice Guideline, 2024 Update, summary → HAPE Diagnosis

versions.note: Names chest congestion, a cough, breathlessness on exertion and a fall in performance, going on to breathlessness at rest and respiratory distress; no blue lips or pink sputum.

source.title: CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → High-altitude pulmonary edema → Diagnosis

facts.claim: High-altitude pulmonary edema usually appears this many days after arriving at a new altitude, and hardly ever after a week of acclimatization there.

source.title: Omidi et al. 2025, What Is New in Altitude- and Cold-Related Illnesses of Travel (a review of the WMS 2024 guideline) → Definitions and epidemiology

facts.claim: High-altitude pulmonary edema can come without any acute mountain sickness before it.

source.title: CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → High-altitude pulmonary edema → Diagnosis

facts.claim: High-altitude pulmonary edema is treated by descent, with as little exertion as possible, since exertion raises the pressure in the arteries of the lungs; supplemental oxygen enough to bring the blood's oxygen saturation above this level, or to relieve the symptoms, treats it too.

source.title: WMS: Acute Altitude Illness Clinical Practice Guideline, 2024 Update, summary → HAPE Treatment

versions.note: Descent urgent and mandatory; oxygen or a portable hyperbaric chamber when immediate descent isn't possible; no saturation target.

source.title: CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → High-altitude pulmonary edema → Treatment

facts.claim: With pulmonary edema, the climber descends at least this far, or until the symptoms go.

source.title: WMS: Acute Altitude Illness Clinical Practice Guideline, 2024 Update, summary → HAPE Treatment

facts.claim: Descend at once: at any suspicion of cerebral edema (ataxia, confusion, drowsiness), at any sign of pulmonary edema, or when acute mountain sickness gets worse in spite of treatment.

source.title: WMS: Acute Altitude Illness Clinical Practice Guideline, 2024 Update, summary → AMS/HACE Treatment, HAPE Treatment
CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → Altitude illness syndromes → Treatment

facts.claim: Supplemental oxygen, at a flow that relieves the symptoms, treats acute mountain sickness, cerebral edema and pulmonary edema; where descent isn't possible it stands in for it, and a severely ill climber breathes it on the way down.

source.title: WMS: Acute Altitude Illness Clinical Practice Guideline, 2024 Update, summary → AMS/HACE Treatment, HAPE Treatment

versions.note: Relieves the headache of acute mountain sickness within about half an hour; critical for cerebral or pulmonary edema when immediate descent isn't possible.

source.title: CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → Altitude illness syndromes → Treatment

facts.claim: A portable hyperbaric chamber, a bag the sick climber is zipped into and pumped up, treats severe altitude illness when descent isn't possible or oxygen isn't to be had; it never delays a descent that is needed, and the climber descends once better.

source.title: WMS: Acute Altitude Illness Clinical Practice Guideline, 2024 Update, summary → AMS/HACE Treatment, HAPE Treatment

versions.note: Oxygen or a portable hyperbaric chamber is critical for cerebral or pulmonary edema when immediate descent isn't possible.

source.title: CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → Altitude illness syndromes → Treatment

facts.claim: A gradual ascent is the first line of prevention: medicines come in beside it when the risk is moderate or high, or when a climber can't ascend gradually, and replace neither the ascent profile nor descent, the single best treatment.

source.title: WMS: Acute Altitude Illness Clinical Practice Guideline, 2024 Update, summary → AMS/HACE Prevention, HAPE Prevention, HAPE Treatment

facts.claim: Acetazolamide speeds up acclimatization: doctors prescribe it to prevent acute mountain sickness, beside a gradual ascent, when the risk is moderate or high, and to treat acute mountain sickness.

source.title: WMS: Acute Altitude Illness Clinical Practice Guideline, 2024 Update, summary → AMS/HACE Prevention, AMS/HACE Treatment

versions.note: Hastens acclimatization and so prevents acute mountain sickness, and helps recovery once symptoms have begun; better validated for prevention than for treatment.

source.title: CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → Medications → Acetazolamide

facts.claim: Dexamethasone treats acute mountain sickness and cerebral edema, and prevents acute mountain sickness (not in children), but it doesn't help acclimatization: a climber treated with it goes no higher until the symptoms stay away without it.

source.title: WMS: Acute Altitude Illness Clinical Practice Guideline, 2024 Update, summary → AMS/HACE Prevention, AMS/HACE Treatment

versions.note: Prevents and treats acute mountain sickness and cerebral edema, and might prevent pulmonary edema; kept for treatment, as an adjunct to descent; stopped at altitude before acclimatization, it can rebound.

source.title: CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → Medications → Dexamethasone

facts.claim: Nifedipine widens the blood vessels and lowers the pressure in the arteries of the lungs: doctors prescribe it to prevent pulmonary edema in climbers who have had it before, and to treat it when descent is impossible or delayed and neither oxygen nor a hyperbaric chamber is to be had.

source.title: WMS: Acute Altitude Illness Clinical Practice Guideline, 2024 Update, summary → HAPE Prevention, HAPE Treatment

versions.note: Prevents and relieves pulmonary edema; for prevention, kept for those particularly susceptible; in treatment an adjunct to descent or oxygen, which are far more effective.

source.title: CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → Medications → Nifedipine
